story.title: ADAEZE AND THE EMPTY CHAIR
story.deck: A dam must start before the rains, and the people it will bury have no vote. Adaeze chairs the hearing; Illuminara has twelve days to find the line between what cannot wait and what cannot be undone.
story.shape: Six scenes across twelve days: a hearing with an empty chair, a refusal between mother and daughter, a night spent breaking one schedule into three columns, a vote taken across three countries, an early storm in a dam gallery, and a seat that is no longer empty.

scenes.title: Item Zero
paragraphs: *Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall · Day One, 09:10*
The chair at the foot of the table was empty on purpose. Ash frame, rush seat, no nameplate. Adaeze had it carried in before the doors opened, and the clerk had entered it in the record as Item Zero.

Seven villages had stood below the old dam until the evacuation order eleven years ago. The order had also dissolved them. Their land was struck from the register, their councils with it, and under Rule Four only communities that occupied mapped ground could vote on the dam that would now be built over their graves.

**Halvard Roos**  
The left abutment gallery is seeping at two point two litres a second. My trigger is six. I will not tell this room the old dam is safe, and I will not tell it the new one can wait for a better hearing.

**Bukola Ferreira**  
Six hundred thousand people drink from this river and the rains come in nineteen days. Every hour spent on ghosts is an hour taken from them.
Adaeze did not look up from her papers. She had chaired basin hearings for twenty years, and she had learned that the quickest way to lose a room was to answer its first insult.

**Adaeze**  
The ghosts have names, Councillor. The clerk will read them at the end of every session until the rule changes. Witness Four, you may begin.

Illuminara had sat at the side table for an hour and no one had addressed her as anything else. That was the arrangement. Her mother had made it in the car, in four sentences, and had not asked whether it suited her.

**Illuminara**  
There are two workable routes for the spillway outfall. The right-bank route is straighter and cheaper, and it carries the outfall and the final spoil dump across the Pell terraces. The left-bank route takes three hundred and ten hectares of irrigated farmland in the Weir Valley and costs nine percent more. Both are safe. Neither is harmless.

**Halvard Roos**  
The contractor says the route must be fixed today. Haul road, spoil and cofferdam are one chain.

**Illuminara**  
That is what the schedule says. I have not yet checked whether it is what the rock says.
Beside the long table the empty chair held the window light. Nobody sat in it. Nobody looked at it either, which was how she knew they had all been counting it.

scenes.title: Rule Four
paragraphs: *Chair's office, Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall · Day One, 12:40*
Adaeze shut the door and took off her glasses, the only sign she gave of how the morning had gone.

**Illuminara**  
I have read all four thousand petitions, from three countries. I can model what each village would choose within a few percent and lodge it as a sealed finding. Then the chair is not empty.

**Adaeze**  
Say the second part again, slowly.

**Illuminara**  
I would not vote for them. I would tell the hearing what they would most probably say.

**Adaeze**  
Nara.
She said it as she had said it when her daughter was twenty-four and new to the courts: not a rebuke, a hand laid flat on a table.

**Adaeze**  
You taught me the first rule of your old trade. The interpreter carries what the speaker says. She does not improve it, and she does not supply it when the speaker is absent.

**Illuminara**  
They are not absent by choice.

**Adaeze**  
That is why it is not yours to supply. You would be the third body to decide for them, and kind about it this time. I have buried that kind of kindness.
*She is right. The model would be accurate, and it would still be a theft.*

**Illuminara**  
Then what do you want from me?

**Adaeze**  
The chair holds a veto and no vote. It can stop what cannot be undone and it cannot start anything. It stays empty until the burial societies choose witnesses to sit in it, and they will need twelve days, because they live in three countries and trust nobody. The room will ask me what those twelve days cost. I need you to tell me. Not what the villages want. Which decisions on that dam are still open if we wait, and which close for ever.

**Illuminara**  
That is an engineering question.

**Adaeze**  
It is the only kind I can take to Councillor Ferreira.
She had walked into the building to offer her mother an answer. She walked out holding a question, and it was the better of the two.

scenes.title: The Chain
paragraphs: *Contractor's site office, Harrow Gorge · Day One, 23:50*

Ruta Kasprzak's schedule ran to four hundred and twelve activities and Illuminara had read every one by ten. She had not found what she wanted because she had been asking the wrong thing. She had asked which tasks were urgent. Her mother had asked which could be undone.
She tagged the schedule again, three questions to a line. Does this move rock? Does this bury ground? Does this build something that must stand on the final choice?
Thirty-one activities survived the third question. Only nine of those touched either route. The rest sat in the chain because, when Ruta wrote the plan, one chain had been the cheapest to haul.

**Ruta Kasprzak**  
You are asking me to double-handle the spoil.

**Illuminara**  
The first two hundred and sixty-two thousand cubic metres must come out before the rains whichever route wins. The cofferdam, the diversion portal and the abutment bolting touch neither the terraces nor the farmland. Only the final dump and the haul road across the terraces do. Send the rock to the old quarry bench instead, and nothing is buried that cannot be dug up again.

**Ruta Kasprzak**  
The bench holds three hundred thousand on the March survey. We've been blasting beside it since.

**Illuminara**  
Then we resurvey at dawn.
Halvard Roos came in at midnight with a flask and no intention of agreeing.

**Halvard Roos**  
You want a delay in my safety case for a legal fiction.

**Illuminara**  
I want a cost in it, not a delay. The temporary haul along the quarry track is slower: nine days of overtime, one point nine million, eleven days of the contractor's float. I have not found a cheaper way, and I am not claiming it is free.

**Halvard Roos**  
And if the rains come early? I have a gallery and a trigger. You have a spreadsheet.
She gave him the limit as exactly as she knew it.

**Illuminara**  
If the gallery crosses your trigger I can carry the shear on the left abutment for about thirty hours. Not twelve days. Thirty hours, and then I fail. The drawdown must do the rest: three point one metres starting tomorrow, which means the city's water is rationed from tomorrow.

**Halvard Roos**  
Then you are not in my safety case.

**Illuminara**  
I did not ask to be. Log it separately.

At dawn the resurvey came back at two hundred and eighty-nine thousand cubic metres, eleven thousand fewer than the March figure. The margin had shrunk from thirty-eight thousand to twenty-seven. It was enough. Halvard read the number twice and wrote it into the log in his own hand.

scenes.title: Three Countries
paragraphs: *Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall, three video links · Day Two, 10:00*

The links came up one at a time: a church hall in Corvane, a school gymnasium in Tessaly, a shipping office in the port of Lisk. Rows of people sat in each of them, and none of them were smiling. For eleven years their burial societies had kept the registers of the dead of all seven villages, and sent money home for funerals when there was no home to bury anyone in.

Adaeze read the proposal into the record: the chair would hold a veto over any work that could not be undone and no affirmative vote; the interval would be twelve days; and the ledger Witness Four had drawn overnight would say, line by line, which works fell on which side.

**Bukola Ferreira**  
This hands strangers a veto over my constituents' water. Whose water do these witnesses drink?

**Adaeze**  
Not yours, Councillor. The veto touches the third column of the ledger only. Rationing, the cofferdam and the foundation go ahead whether the chair is filled or not.

**Mirela Haddad, from Corvane**  
Witness Four. Which route buries the Pell terraces?

**Illuminara**  
The right-bank route. The final dump covers the lower three terraces. I would choose the left-bank route for that reason, and it takes farmland from people sitting in this room. I am not the one to weigh those losses against each other.

**Mirela Haddad, from Corvane**  
Good. Then you will say the same thing to our engineer. We want one of our own to read your numbers, paid from the hearing's budget, with the right to survey the bench ourselves.

**Adaeze**  
Granted.

**Bukola Ferreira**  
The valley will want the same.

**Adaeze**  
The valley has the same. Mr Roos answers to the safety authority, not to them. Hire whom you like.

The council voted six to three. Adaeze, who did not vote, asked that the record show the proposal had been hers, and that whatever blame followed it was hers also. Bukola Ferreira looked at her for a long moment, and then, to her own evident annoyance, nodded.

scenes.title: Thirty Hours
paragraphs: *Left abutment gallery, old Harrow Gorge dam · Day Eleven, 02:40*

The storm came eight days early: a hundred and forty millimetres in nine hours. The drawdown had bought three metres of freeboard and cost the city eleven days of rationing. Up on the quarry bench, under tarpaulins, lay two hundred and forty-seven thousand cubic metres of rock that had not yet been promised to anyone's land.
At 02:40 the gallery drain read six point one litres a second.

**Halvard Roos, over the radio**  
It's crossed. Illuminara. Now.

She went in as far as the third joint. The concrete sweated cold. She laid both palms on the wall, found the plane along which the abutment wanted to slide, and began to carry what the rock had stopped carrying. It was not like lifting. It was like standing in a river that wished her to step aside.
She had told him thirty hours. She did not look at the clock.

**Halvard Roos, over the radio**  
Five point four. Falling. Keep going.
*Not for ever. Only until the drawdown is the stronger thing.*

At hour nineteen the rain stopped. The reading fell to two point nine and held there. Halvard came down the gallery himself, in a rain cape with the flask in his pocket, and stood beside her until she took her hands from the wall.

**Halvard Roos**  
I can take it from here.

**Illuminara**  
Write it down.

**Halvard Roos**  
I already have. Nineteen hours, in a separate column. You are still not in my safety case.
She sat on the gallery floor. She could not feel her hands, and would not for six hours. Halvard unscrewed the flask and held it out, and she took it with both wrists.

scenes.title: The Seat
paragraphs: *Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall · Day Twelve, 10:00*

The witnesses had travelled through the night from three countries. They took the chair in turn, as the rule required, and the first to sit was an old man who lowered himself into it with one hand on the rush seat as if it might not hold.
Their engineer had read the bench survey and the gallery log. She had asked for nothing to be changed.

**Tomasz Brandl**  
Pell uses the veto on the right-bank route. We will not be under the dump. I carry Pell's register, not Quill's, and the next witness will carry theirs. We do not choose the left-bank route either. That land is the valley's, and so is the choice.

**Bukola Ferreira**  
I read the gallery log on the way here, all of it, for the first time in my career. The valley will take the left-bank route if the levy pays for the land at full value. We do not like it. We will sign it.

**Adaeze**  
Then the record will show two decisions made by the people they bind, and none by anyone else.

By noon the cofferdam stood across the diversion portal, the foundation excavation was within a day of its first schedule, and Rule Four had been amended: a dissolved community kept a seat at every hearing on the land it had lost, with a veto over works that could not be undone and a binding say over its resettlement and its access to the river. The Valley Courier called Adaeze a sentimentalist. The newsletter of the Lisk camp called her a bureaucrat. She read both and had them filed.
Illuminara waited at the door, her hands wrapped in gauze because Halvard had insisted.

**Adaeze**  
Nara. You are late.

**Illuminara**  
I was holding up your dam.

**Adaeze**  
I know. I read the log.

Her mother crossed the hall, took the gauzed hands in both of hers, and looked at them for a moment without saying whether she thought the cost had been fair. Then she let go and went to find the carpenter. The chair, she had decided, would be fixed to the floor.

The left-bank route takes three hundred and ten hectares of irrigated farmland in the Weir Valley and costs nine percent more. Both are safe. Neither is harmless.

**Halvard Roos**  
The contractor says the route must be fixed today. Haul road, spoil and cofferdam are one chain.

**Illuminara**  
That is what the schedule says. I have not yet checked whether it is what the rock says.
Beside the long table the empty chair held the window light. Nobody sat in it. Nobody looked at it either, which was how she knew they had all been counting it.

scenes.title: Rule Four
paragraphs: *Chair's office, Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall · Day One, 12:40*
Adaeze shut the door and took off her glasses, the only sign she gave of how the morning had gone.

**Illuminara**  
I have read all four thousand petitions, from three countries. I can model what each village would choose within a few percent and lodge it as a sealed finding. Then the chair is not empty.

**Adaeze**  
Say the second part again, slowly.

**Illuminara**  
I would not vote for them. I would tell the hearing what they would most probably say.

**Adaeze**  
Nara.
She said it as she had said it when her daughter was twenty-four and new to the courts: not a rebuke, a hand laid flat on a table.

**Adaeze**  
You taught me the first rule of your old trade. The interpreter carries what the speaker says. She does not improve it, and she does not supply it when the speaker is absent.

**Illuminara**  
They are not absent by choice.

**Adaeze**  
That is why it is not yours to supply. You would be the third body to decide for them, and kind about it this time. I have buried that kind of kindness.
*She is right. The model would be accurate, and it would still be a theft.*

**Illuminara**  
Then what do you want from me?

**Adaeze**  
The chair holds a veto and no vote. It can stop what cannot be undone and it cannot start anything. It stays empty until the burial societies choose witnesses to sit in it, and they will need twelve days, because they live in three countries and trust nobody. The room will ask me what those twelve days cost. I need you to tell me. Not what the villages want. Which decisions on that dam are still open if we wait, and which close for ever.

**Illuminara**  
That is an engineering question.

**Adaeze**  
It is the only kind I can take to Councillor Ferreira.
She had walked into the building to offer her mother an answer. She walked out holding a question, and it was the better of the two.

scenes.title: The Chain
paragraphs: *Contractor's site office, Harrow Gorge · Day One, 23:50*
Ruta Kasprzak's schedule ran to four hundred and twelve activities; Illuminara read them by ten. She had been asking which tasks were urgent. Adaeze had asked which could be undone.

She tagged each line with three questions. Does this move rock? Bury ground? Build something that must stand on the final choice? Thirty-one activities survived the third question. Nine touched either route. The rest formed one chain because it was cheapest to haul.

**Ruta Kasprzak**  
Line one hundred and eighty-four. Batching-plant pad. You put it in the middle column, reversible at a price.

**Illuminara**  
The slab can be broken out.

**Ruta Kasprzak**  
The forty anchor piles cross the right-bank haul alignment. Break the slab and the piles remain under whichever road loses. Pull them and I lose two days and nine hundred thousand.
Illuminara moved the row into the third column. The nine became ten.

**Illuminara**  
Then no piles until the route is chosen. Put the mobile plant on ballast. Add two days to concrete production and the nine hundred thousand to the hearing ledger.

**Ruta Kasprzak**  
You concede quickly for someone who read all four hundred and twelve.

**Illuminara**  
The ledger is useful only if the person who finds me wrong can change it.
Ruta tapped the column heading with one blunt fingernail. Illuminara added a blank beside every classification: challenger, evidence, time filed. No one had asked her for that column.

**Ruta Kasprzak**  
You are still asking me to double-handle the spoil.

**Illuminara**  
The first two hundred and sixty-two thousand cubic metres must come out before the rains whichever route wins. The cofferdam, diversion portal and abutment bolting touch neither the terraces nor the farmland. Only the final dump and the haul road across the terraces do. Send the rock to the old quarry bench instead, and nothing is buried that cannot be dug up again.

**Ruta Kasprzak**  
The bench holds three hundred thousand on the March survey. We've been blasting beside it since.

**Illuminara**  
Then we resurvey at dawn.
Halvard Roos came in at midnight with a flask and no intention of agreeing.

**Halvard Roos**  
You want a delay in my safety case for a legal fiction.

**Illuminara**  
I want a cost in it, not a delay. The temporary haul along the quarry track is slower: nine days of overtime, one point nine million, eleven days of the contractor's float. I have not found a cheaper way, and I am not claiming it is free.

**Halvard Roos**  
And if the rains come early? I have a gallery and a trigger. You have a spreadsheet.

**Illuminara**  
If the gallery crosses your trigger I can carry the shear on the left abutment for about thirty hours. Not twelve days. Thirty hours, and then I fail. The drawdown must do the rest: three point one metres starting tomorrow, which means the city's water is rationed from tomorrow.

**Halvard Roos**  
Then you are not in my safety case.

**Illuminara**  
I did not ask to be. Log it separately.

At dawn the resurvey came back at two hundred and eighty-nine thousand cubic metres, leaving twenty-seven thousand above the excavation target, three thousand short of Halvard's minimum reserve. Ruta leased a rail-yard stockpile for the final three thousand at a further hundred and eighty thousand. Halvard read both numbers twice and wrote them into the log in his own hand.

scenes.title: Three Countries
paragraphs: *Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall, three video links · Day Two, 10:00*

The links came up: a church hall in Corvane, a school gym in Tessaly, a shipping office in Lisk. For eleven years their burial societies had kept the seven villages' registers and sent money home for funerals when there was no home to return to.
Adaeze read the motion: an empty chair, a veto over irreversible work, no affirmative vote, a twelve-day interval and Illuminara's line-by-line ledger.

**Bukola Ferreira**  
This hands strangers a veto over my constituents' water. Whose water do these witnesses drink?

**Adaeze**  
Not yours. The veto touches only the third column. Rationing, the cofferdam and the foundation proceed.

**Mirela Haddad, from Corvane**  
And who owns the third column? Witness Four? Your safety authority?
Illuminara turned the ledger so all three cameras could see the blank beside every row.

**Illuminara**  
The safety authority classifies first. The chair's engineer may contest a row within twenty-four hours. The more irreversible reading governs until a reasoned ruling. Ruta found the row that proved the challenge belongs.

**Mirela Haddad, from Corvane**  
Then our engineer, paid by the hearing, reads your numbers and surveys the bench.

**Halvard Roos**  
If the gallery reaches its trigger while a row is disputed, protective work cannot wait.

**Illuminara**  
Only the work necessary to take the reading below the trigger, logged by the hour and reviewed the next day. The exception cannot choose a route.

**Savitri Moyo, from the Weir Valley**  
Same terms for us. Nobody here accepts the left bank for the valley. We meet on Day Eleven; record the dissent.

**Bukola Ferreira**  
Return the rule's operation to public hearing after one year. I can defend bounded delay, not invent a valley choice.

**Adaeze**  
Put both conditions in the motion.

**Mirela Haddad, from Corvane**  
Witness Four. Which route buries the Pell terraces?

**Illuminara**  
The right-bank route covers the lower three Pell terraces. I would choose the left for that reason, but it takes this hearing's farmland. I do not weigh those losses.

**Bukola Ferreira**  
My vote is yes, with the one-year review. The valley's vote remains its own.
The tally closed six to three. Rule Four took effect at noon. Adaeze, who did not vote, put her authorship and any blame into the record.

scenes.title: Thirty Hours
paragraphs: *Left abutment gallery, old Harrow Gorge dam · Day Eleven, 02:40*

The storm came nine days early: a hundred and forty millimetres in nine hours. The drawdown had bought three metres of freeboard and cost the city eleven days of rationing, but the sudden rise drove reservoir pressure through the known joint in the left abutment faster than the drains could clear it. Of the two hundred and sixty-two thousand cubic metres due out before the expected rains, two hundred and forty-seven thousand lay on the quarry bench. The remaining fifteen thousand was still rock in the river-side cut; the storm had arrived before its excavation shift.
At 02:40 the gallery drain read six point one litres a second.

**Halvard Roos, over the radio**  
It's crossed. Illuminara. Now.

She went in as far as the third joint. The concrete sweated cold. She laid both palms on the wall, found the plane along which the abutment wanted to slide, and began to carry what the rock had stopped carrying. It was not like lifting. It was like standing in a river that wished her to step aside.
She had told him thirty hours. She did not look at the clock.

**Halvard Roos, over the radio**  
Five point four. Falling. Keep going.
*Not for ever. Only until the drawdown is the stronger thing.*

At hour nineteen the reservoir inflow passed its crest. With the rain already gone and the reservoir three metres lower than it would otherwise have been, the drains took the load back. The reading fell to two point nine and held there. Halvard came down the gallery himself, in a rain cape with the flask in his pocket, and stood beside her until she took her hands from the wall.

**Halvard Roos**  
I can take it from here.

**Illuminara**  
Write it down.

**Halvard Roos**  
I already have. Nineteen hours, in a separate column. You are still not in my safety case.
She sat on the gallery floor. She could not feel her hands, and would not for six hours. Halvard unscrewed the flask and held it out, and she took it with both wrists.

scenes.title: The Seat
paragraphs: *Harrow Gorge Hearing Hall · Day Twelve, 10:00*
The witnesses had travelled through the night from three countries. They took the chair in turn. First, an old man lowered himself with one hand on the rush seat as if it might not hold.
Their engineers had read the bench survey, challenged two ledger rows and accepted the written rulings.

**Tomasz Brandl**  
Pell vetoes the right-bank route. We will not be under the dump. I carry Pell's register, not Quill's; the next witness carries theirs. We do not choose the left bank. That is the valley's land and choice.

**Savitri Moyo**  
At four this morning, thirty-eight of fifty-one landholding households chose the left bank with full-value purchase and the levy. Nine refused. Four abstained. I voted no. I carry the result because it is ours, not because it is mine.

**Bukola Ferreira**  
My city paid eleven rationing days. I put the levy on today's council docket. I do not cast the valley's vote.

**Adaeze**  
Then the record will show two decisions made by the people they bind, and none by anyone else.

Rule Four had stood amended since Day Two; today was its first use. Two disputed rows were settled before the storm, and Halvard's emergency log chose no route. By noon the cofferdam stood and excavation was within a day of schedule.
The Valley Courier called Adaeze a sentimentalist. The newsletter of the Lisk camp called her a bureaucrat. She read both and had them filed.
Illuminara waited at the door, her hands wrapped in gauze because Halvard had insisted.

**Adaeze**  
Nara. You are late.

**Illuminara**  
I was holding up your dam.

**Adaeze**  
I know. I read the log. And the fourth column.

Her mother crossed the hall, took the gauzed hands in both of hers, and looked at them for a moment without saying whether she thought the cost had been fair. Then she let go and went to find the carpenter. The chair, she had decided, would be fixed to the floor. The ledger would remain loose enough to turn.
